newsitem.title: UK: AIDS campaigns in poor states fail most women.
newsitem.headline: AIDS campaigns in poor states fail most women.

text.p: AIDS prevention programmes in developing nations fail to address the problems facing married women, who are the people most at risk, a German-based expert said on Friday.

"When a woman is economically powerless to negotiate her basic needs, or is subject to domestic violence and abuse, encouraging her to negotiate safer sex is unrealistic," Doris D'Cruz-Grote wrote in this week's Lancet medical magazine.

She said a review showed programmes in developing nations sought to reduce the spread of infection by targeting high-risk groups, such as prostitutes, by reducing the number of sexual partners and by promoting condom use.

But D'Cruz-Grote, an expert in the HIV virus that causes AIDS, said this failed to address the problems facing those most at risk, in particular women with one sexual partner who made up 50 to 70 percent of all infected women in Africa.
"Most women in need of prevention are not sex workers but women with one partner -- their husband. For them monogamy is an irrelevant strategy," she wrote.
What was needed to limit the spread of HIV was comprehensive sex education and sexual health services offering counselling, contraception and treatment for sexually transmitted diseases, she said.
But ultimately, the social and economic status of vulnerable groups must be improved for HIV prevention to work.
